title: Stoic week
hook: modern Stoics run a week-long practice experiment

segments.voice: Yesterday, the secular sabbath, a weekly margin with nothing to produce. Your line was a rest day. Is it in the calendar, and does someone else know? Day one thousand four hundred thirteen.

A sign-up form, an online handbook, a short reading for each morning, a set of questions for each night. Far from Athens, and long after it, a group of modern Stoic teachers and researchers runs a week of Stoic practice, open to anyone who wants to try it. People from different jobs and countries do the same exercises on the same days, then report back how the week went. It is part course, part experiment. Back in year two, this path spent a long stretch with the Stoics, from a Stoic morning to a year on the porch. Today the porch opens again, but this time as a test you run on yourself, for one week.
screen: `A HANDBOOK, A MORNING, A NIGHT.` → `PART COURSE, PART EXPERIMENT.` → `THE PORCH OPENS AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Tradition says the Stoics took their name from a painted porch in Athens, the Stoa, where Zeno taught in public. So the porch was never a temple. It was a place people walked past, and some stopped to listen. A Stoic week keeps that spirit: the practice happens in ordinary life, at the desk and the dinner table. It rests on three old habits. First, the morning preview. Marcus Aurelius wrote in his notebook, "Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial." It sounds gloomy. It isn't. He goes on to say none of them can harm his character, and that he was made to work alongside them. The preview is a way of not being ambushed. Second, the sorting through the day. Epictetus opens his handbook with a plain sentence: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not." Your judgments and choices are in your power. The traffic, the weather and other people's moods are not. All day long, a Stoic week asks: which pile is this in? Third, the evening review. Seneca describes ending each day by questioning himself, in paraphrase: what bad habit did I cure today, what fault did I resist, in what way am I better? Not a trial. More like a coach replaying the tape. Notice the shape: prepare, sort, review. It is small enough to try for seven days, and that's the point. A week turns the porch from something you read about into something you can check.
screen: `THE PORCH WAS IN PUBLIC.` · `MORNING: NOT BEING AMBUSHED.` · `DAY: WHICH PILE IS THIS IN?` · `EVENING: REPLAY THE TAPE.` · then, large: `PREPARE, SORT, REVIEW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: try a Stoic day again, starting now. Settle, and breathe slowly. Run the morning preview for whatever is left of today. Who or what might test you? Name it plainly. Then take one thing that worries you and sort it. What part is in your power, your judgment, your response? What part isn't? Let the second pile rest where it is. Hold the first pile lightly, like a tool you'll pick up later. The bell holds the time.
Stoic week. A week of Stoic practice run by modern Stoics and open to anyone: a morning preview, sorting through the day, an evening review. Today's word.

Your line: the porch again. Today, each time something irritates you, the traffic, a message, a delay, stop and ask which pile it's in: in my power, or not. Then put your effort only where it can land. Day one thousand four hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Modern Stoics run a week of practice open to the public, with a handbook, a morning reading and preview, exercises for sorting what is and isn't in one's power during the day, and an evening review; many people also keep these habits on their own.

notes: The modern Stoic week (run by the Modern Stoicism group) is described without dates, participant counts or results. The index says it is 'annual'; the script leaves that out under the claims rule. Confirm the description (handbook, morning and evening exercises, open sign-up, participants report back) is accurate.
The naming of the Stoics after the Stoa Poikile, where Zeno taught, is given as 'tradition says' (Diogenes Laertius 7.5). Confirm the reference.
Seneca's evening review is paraphrased from De Ira 3.36. Confirm the three questions are a fair paraphrase.
Check the Long 1862 wording of Meditations 2.1 and the Long 1877 wording of Enchiridion 1 against a scan.
The 'year two' reference points to the Stoic stretch on this path (y2 days 677–685, ending 'A year on the porch').

Editor pass: Seneca's three questions re-paraphrased to follow De Ira 3.36 (habit cured, fault resisted, how better) instead of a well/badly formula; 'the sentence the whole school leans on' (a claim about the whole school) became 'a plain sentence', in teach and trapdoor; the carry moved from a second nightly three-question review (repeating day 1406's Zengzi carry) to sorting irritations into the two piles.
